events.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and blast radius for auth-service around 2026-04-22. Determine: (1) exact onset time when auth-service p99 latency began rising toward ~3.8s and 503s on /v1/auth/login appeared; (2) whether the latency is code-path-specific (only login/verifyPassword) or affects all auth-service endpoints and health checks; (3) resource trends on auth-service at onset (CPU, memory, thread/connection saturation), to distinguish CPU-bound work from blocked/waiting calls; (4) whether any OTHER service shows a similar onset/latency pattern in the same window. Report raw error signatures and percentiles, not just summaries.

Enumerate ALL changes that could plausibly affect the login path, across the whole fleet, in the 24-72h before the reported time: get_deployments and get_config_changes for auth-service AND for every service auth-service depends on. Use get_service_dependencies to map auth-service's login-path dependencies (DB, cache, token/session store, etc.) and identify shared components those dependencies and auth-service have in common. Also search_historical_incidents for last year's bcrypt regression to capture its signature (what it looked like, how it was detected, how it was fixed) so we can compare against the current symptom.

With the onset time from task a and the dependency map/changes from task b, correlate: determine whether the auth-service onset aligns in time with a change to auth-service itself, or with a change/degradation in an upstream-of-auth-service dependency or shared component. Specifically check dependencies' metrics at the onset window (errors, latency, saturation) and confirm or rule out that auth-service latency is downstream-propagated rather than locally caused. Also test the bcrypt-regression signature: is the slowness concentrated in password-verification CPU time (consistent with bcrypt) versus blocked/waiting (consistent with a downstream dependency)?

events.statement: No auth-service deployment exists anywhere in the 2026-04-16T00:00Z -> 2026-04-22T08:59Z window (and none in the narrower 2026-04-19T07:00Z -> 2026-04-22T08:59Z window either): get_deployments for auth-service returned count 0, and the all-services query returned a single deployment belonging to portfolio-service.

The only config change in the whole window that touches auth-service is cfg-2801: key log.level changed INFO->WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume') — a logging verbosity change, not an auth/bcrypt/crypto parameter. No other config changes exist fleet-wide in the window.

The historical bcrypt precedent HIST-101 (2025-08-14) has the same symptom signature as the current report — 'login p99 4s', '503 on login', 'high cpu' — with root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', category bad_deployment, resolved by 'Rolled back v6.4.0'. It is a matching lead only, not current evidence.

Because the bcrypt precedent required a release to raise the cost factor, and there is no auth-service release in this window, the current incident cannot be the same deployment-driven mechanism unless data outside this window is involved — the change history points away from an auth-service code/config cause.

auth-service's login path depends on: user-db (postgres, kind=db), redis-cache (redis, kind=cache, marked shared=true — 'shared' datastores are used by several services), kyc-provider (external, has_telemetry=false), and is called by api-gateway (kind=http). redis-cache being shared with several services is a candidate vector for damage originating outside auth-service.

Prior incident HIST-107 ('Cold cache storm after redis failover', 2025-12-09, services redis-cache + market-data-service, root cause 'Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica') shows the shared redis-cache has a history of degrading its consumers — a second, non-bcrypt lead consistent with a shared-dependency cause.

events.description: Could not run the upstream dependency query for redis-cache (get_service_dependencies on redis-cache, direction=upstream) — it was rejected with budget_exhausted, so I never received the caller list for the shared redis-cache.

Deployment and config change queries were sent but I could not enumerate changes for user-db, redis-cache, api-gateway or kyc-provider as separate per-service queries; only the fleet-wide scope queries ran (which returned just dep-5803 and cfg-2801).

No deployment/config history was retrieved for the 24-72h period beyond 2026-04-16T00:00Z (i.e. before 2026-04-19), so any change older than ~3.5 days that could affect login (e.g. user-db schema/index migration, redis caching-layer config) is not covered.
kyc-provider is an external node with has_telemetry=false, so no deployment, config or metric data can be obtained for it.

events.answer: Across the 24-72h window (2026-04-16 to 2026-04-22T08:59Z) the fleet shows NO auth-service deployment and only one config change touching auth-service (log.level INFO->WARN at 03:40Z, cosmetic) plus one unrelated portfolio-service deploy. So the change history does NOT support the reported "bcrypt regression after a release" pattern: last year's HIST-101 signature was a login release raising bcrypt cost 10->14, detected by the same symptoms (login p99 4s, 503s, high CPU) and fixed by rolling back v6.4.0. The current incident has no auth-service release to roll back; the plausible change surface is elsewhere (shared dependencies).

events.statement: auth-service p99 latency was flat ~85-95ms until 06:53Z, then jumped at 06:54Z to 3849.2ms and stayed ~3.5-4.0s through 08:59Z. The 4s bucket avg reported at 06:52 is a bucket artifact: the 60s-bucket zoom shows 06:52 = 93.19ms and the jump is exactly at 06:54Z (=3849.2ms).

503s on POST /v1/auth/login are NOT bad-password/verify failures: every 503 is logged as an overload rejection. Top error pattern 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)' count=372, first_seen 2026-04-22T06:55:42Z, last 08:58:57Z; error_rate jumped from ~0.2% (06:48) to 3.43% avg/13.19% max in the 06:52 bucket and ~14% sustained thereafter, with total_matched=372 ERROR entries (returned 30 of 372, truncated=true).

At onset auth-service worker pool was fully saturated with a large waiting backlog, not CPU-idle: 32 WARN 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=...)' entries starting 06:54:53Z with queue depths of 3787-98763 (e.g. queue=39035, 94198, 98763); the first 503 at 06:55:42Z is the accept-queue-full rejection that follows.

auth-service CPU saturated simultaneously with the latency jump: cpu_pct ~37-40% through 06:45, then 06:50 avg=71.88 max=96.96 and ~96-98% from 06:55 onward (max 99.54), while memory_pct stayed flat ~51-53% (max 57.07) — a CPU-bound signature with no memory growth.

auth-service request_rate more than tripled at onset: ~391-411 req/s baseline (06:00-06:45) to avg 680.57/max 1012.36 at 06:50 and ~1450-1520 req/s sustained afterward — a traffic surge coincides with the CPU saturation, and the autoscaler could not absorb it: 'autoscaler: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' (first 06:57:15Z, count=4).

Only /v1/auth/login appears in the auth-service failure logs (all 372 ERRORs are that endpoint's accept-queue rejections); no health-check, verifyPassword-specific, or other-endpoint error signature appears in the returned log window.

events.description: Per-endpoint / health-check breakdown was not queried directly; only overall latency_p99_ms and error_rate exist in auth-service available_metrics, so I could not numerically confirm health checks were unaffected (only log evidence that login is the sole failing path).
No cross-service comparison was run for other services in the 06:45-07:00Z window (blast radius question 4).
The auth-service log query for 06:45-07:10Z returned truncated=true (84 matched, 40 shown) and the ERROR query truncated=true (372 matched, 30 shown); no full listing of WARN/INFO beyond patterns.

events.answer: Onset is 06:54Z: auth-service p99 jumped in a single minute from ~89ms (06:53) to 3849.2ms (06:54), with the first 503 'accept queue full' on POST /v1/auth/login at 06:55:42Z — the 4s average in the 06:52 coarse bucket is a bucket artifact, not an earlier onset. The failure is an overload/saturation signature: worker pool saturated at active=64/64 with queues up to ~98k, CPU pinned at 96-99% (memory flat ~52%), request_rate tripled from ~400 to ~1500 req/s, and the autoscaler was capped at maxReplicas 8 versus desired 14. CPU-bound saturation (not a blocked/password-hash-specific code path) is what the data shows, and every observed 503 is a queue-full rejection rather than a verifyPassword/bcrypt failure.

events.statement: redis-cache (shared cache in auth-service login path) shows NO degradation at the auth-service onset: cpu_pct stayed flat 20.59-23.97% (06:40 avg 21.96 -> 06:54 avg 21.95) and hit_ratio_pct stayed ~94.4-97.3% (06:52 96.15, 06:54 96.09) through the whole window. The dependency is healthy on CPU and hit ratio across 06:40-07:20.

user-db connections_active jumped at the same onset bucket but is a downstream consequence, not a saturated upstream: it rose from ~25 (06:40-06:50) to avg 73.31/max 74.03 at 06:52 and ~79 sustained, with slow_queries_per_min flat at 0.18-0.51 the entire time (06:54 avg 0.41). No slow-query or DB-saturation signature exists.

auth-service CPU saturation begins in the 06:52 120s bucket (avg 96.89, max 96.96, after 34.42 at 06:50), i.e. one 120s bucket BEFORE the latency p99 jump recorded at 06:54 (avg 3759.86 / max 3849.2, after 91.5 at 06:52). Local CPU is pinned well before/at the same time as measured latency, not after it.

auth-service latency is flat ~85-94ms for 06:40-06:52 and then jumps in one step to ~3.5-4.0s sustained through 07:20 (min 83.49, max 4015.31) - a local step change at its own CPU saturation, not a gradual ramp consistent with a downstream dependency slowing down.

Neither login-path dependency shows an error/latency/saturation signal at the onset: redis-cache CPU ~22% and hit ratio ~96% flat, user-db slow_queries_per_min ~0.3 flat; the only rising upstream-facing number (user-db connections_active) rises simultaneously with auth-service CPU/latency, consistent with auth-service itself driving the extra connections during its own saturation. This points to a locally-caused (in-auth-service) saturation rather than downstream-propagated latency.

The bcrypt-regression signature (slowness concentrated in password-verification CPU time) is NOT distinguishable from the observed data because auth-service CPU is pegged at 96-99% while memory stays flat - consistent with CPU-bound work in general - but no metric separates verifyPassword CPU from other CPU; the queue-saturation logs (active=64/64, queues up to 98763) and the 372 accept-queue-full 503s reported by T1 are an overload/queueing signature rather than a per-hash CPU-time signature. Ruling out blocked/waiting: no dependency shows elevated latency or saturation to blame, and auth CPU saturates simultaneously.

events.description: Could not check auth-service's per-endpoint or downgraded-path CPU breakdown (e.g. verifyPassword CPU vs other handlers) - auth-service exposes only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts; no CPU-time-by-code-path metric exists.
Did not check whether api-gateway or any other caller/co-tenant service shows a similar latency/CPU onset in the same window (blast-radius cross-check beyond dependencies).

Did not retrieve redis-cache connected_clients/evictions_per_min or user-db cpu_pct/replication_lag_ms at the onset - only redis cpu_pct/hit_ratio and user-db connections_active/slow_queries_per_min were queried.

events.answer: Auth-service's onset aligns with a change in auth-service itself, not with an upstream dependency: its own CPU saturates (96.89% at 06:52, 34% at 06:50) at/before the one-step p99 jump to 3849.2ms at 06:54, while login-path dependencies stay flat (redis-cache ~22% CPU, ~96% hit ratio; user-db slow queries ~0.3/min). Only user-db connections_active rises, simultaneously with auth CPU, consistent with auth-service driving it during its own saturation rather than being slowed by it - so the latency is locally caused, not downstream-propagated. The data shows a CPU-bound overload/queueing signature (CPU pinned, memory flat, queue-full 503s) but does not isolate bcrypt/verifyPassword CPU time, so the bcrypt-regression claim cannot be confirmed from these metrics.

Shared-infrastructure/co-tenant contention (node/sidecar/shared cache) degraded auth-service indirectly

tasks.answer: Onset is 06:54Z: auth-service p99 jumped in a single minute from ~89ms (06:53) to 3849.2ms (06:54), with the first 503 'accept queue full' on POST /v1/auth/login at 06:55:42Z — the 4s average in the 06:52 coarse bucket is a bucket artifact, not an earlier onset. The failure is an overload/saturation signature: worker pool saturated at active=64/64 with queues up to ~98k, CPU pinned at 96-99% (memory flat ~52%), request_rate tripled from ~400 to ~1500 req/s, and the autoscaler was capped at maxReplicas 8 versus desired 14. CPU-bound saturation (not a blocked/password-hash-specific code path) is what the data shows, and every observed 503 is a queue-full rejection rather than a verifyPassword/bcrypt failure.

tasks.objective: Enumerate ALL changes that could plausibly affect the login path, across the whole fleet, in the 24-72h before the reported time: get_deployments and get_config_changes for auth-service AND for every service auth-service depends on. Use get_service_dependencies to map auth-service's login-path dependencies (DB, cache, token/session store, etc.) and identify shared components those dependencies and auth-service have in common. Also search_historical_incidents for last year's bcrypt regression to capture its signature (what it looked like, how it was detected, how it was fixed) so we can compare against the current symptom.
tasks.answer: Across the 24-72h window (2026-04-16 to 2026-04-22T08:59Z) the fleet shows NO auth-service deployment and only one config change touching auth-service (log.level INFO->WARN at 03:40Z, cosmetic) plus one unrelated portfolio-service deploy. So the change history does NOT support the reported "bcrypt regression after a release" pattern: last year's HIST-101 signature was a login release raising bcrypt cost 10->14, detected by the same symptoms (login p99 4s, 503s, high CPU) and fixed by rolling back v6.4.0. The current incident has no auth-service release to roll back; the plausible change surface is elsewhere (shared dependencies).

tasks.objective: With the onset time from task a and the dependency map/changes from task b, correlate: determine whether the auth-service onset aligns in time with a change to auth-service itself, or with a change/degradation in an upstream-of-auth-service dependency or shared component. Specifically check dependencies' metrics at the onset window (errors, latency, saturation) and confirm or rule out that auth-service latency is downstream-propagated rather than locally caused. Also test the bcrypt-regression signature: is the slowness concentrated in password-verification CPU time (consistent with bcrypt) versus blocked/waiting (consistent with a downstream dependency)?
tasks.answer: Auth-service's onset aligns with a change in auth-service itself, not with an upstream dependency: its own CPU saturates (96.89% at 06:52, 34% at 06:50) at/before the one-step p99 jump to 3849.2ms at 06:54, while login-path dependencies stay flat (redis-cache ~22% CPU, ~96% hit ratio; user-db slow queries ~0.3/min). Only user-db connections_active rises, simultaneously with auth CPU, consistent with auth-service driving it during its own saturation rather than being slowed by it - so the latency is locally caused, not downstream-propagated. The data shows a CPU-bound overload/queueing signature (CPU pinned, memory flat, queue-full 503s) but does not isolate bcrypt/verifyPassword CPU time, so the bcrypt-regression claim cannot be confirmed from these metrics.
